c.text: **Speech is a complex learned skill.** Children learn to coordinate their speech organs with little explicit instruction and very little visual feedback about what those organs are doing.
children: A child can develop a large vocabulary and near-adult language between about two and four years of age. Reading and writing whole words develop later and require much more explicit instruction.

c.text: **Articulatory phonetics** studies how structures in the vocal tract move to produce speech. The tongue and lips must make coordinated movements to produce different sounds.
**Speech technology** attempts to model this human ability. Understanding human speech and understanding how AI models speech are connected questions.

c.text: **Acoustic phonetics** studies speech sounds, including how air vibrates in the vocal tract. The vocal tract is the air passage shaped by the tongue and the surrounding structures.
children: The passage can be represented as a straight column of air to make its vibration easier to study. Straightening the drawing simplifies the shape of the model.

c.text: **AI literacy means understanding how AI systems operate.** Knowing how to build or use a system does not necessarily explain how its behavior arises.
AI has psychological, economic, social and environmental harms, as well as potential benefits in areas such as medicine and environmental engineering.
children: Understanding these systems helps people assess their benefits and harms. This matters for scientists using AI, politicians developing rules and lawyers dealing with its consequences.

c.text: Understanding **human speech**, **basic physical principles** and **AI models of cognition** connects several kinds of knowledge. Speech can be studied as a cognitive skill, a physical process and a skill that a computer attempts to model.

**Elementary programming** develops methodical reasoning. Working across linguistics, physics, psychology, biology and computer science also develops the ability to connect ideas and use AI more thoughtfully.

c.text: **Diotima’s ladder** distinguishes memorization and repetition from creative understanding. **Creative reasoning** asks how ideas relate. Similar-looking things can work differently, and different-looking things can share an underlying principle.
children: Asking and answering questions develops this kind of understanding. It involves posing problems, solving them, reading critically and explaining ideas rather than only repeating them.

c.text: **Voicing** means whether the vocal folds vibrate. The sounds in each pair keep the same place of articulation while changing voicing.
children: The pairs are f and v, th in “thing” and th in “that,” s and z, and sh in “mesh” and the sound in “beige.” The second sound in each pair is voiced.

c.text: **Place of articulation** identifies where the vocal tract is narrowed. Moving from one pair to another changes that location. Voicing and place therefore describe different properties of a consonant.

c.text: **Fricatives** are produced by sending air through a narrow opening. Their classification combines **place of articulation** with **voicing**.
children: **Labial** f and v use the lip region. **Dental** th sounds use the teeth. **Alveolar** s and z use the ridge just behind the upper teeth. **Postalveolar** sh and the sound in “beige” are produced farther back.

c.text: Each place has a voiceless and a voiced member. For example, f and v share their place but differ in whether the vocal folds vibrate.

c.text: A **stop** involves a complete closure in the mouth. The place of that closure distinguishes three groups.
children: The lips close for **p, b and m**. The tongue tip closes at the alveolar ridge for **t, d and n**. The back of the tongue closes at the velum, or soft palate, for **k, g and ng**.

c.text: Among the **oral stops**, p, t and k are voiceless, while b, d and g are voiced. Air is released through the mouth when the closure opens.
The **nasal stops** m, n and ng keep the mouth closed while air escapes through the nose. The **velum** lowers to open that route.
children: For example, d and n are both voiced and alveolar. Their difference is the oral or nasal route taken by the air.

c.text: Consonants are organized by **voicing**, **place of articulation** and **manner of articulation**. Voicing concerns vocal-fold vibration, place concerns where the mouth is narrowed or closed, and manner concerns how air passes through.
children: **Fricatives** allow air through a narrow gap. **Oral stops**, also called **plosives**, close the mouth passage and release air through it. **Nasal stops** close the mouth passage while letting air leave through the nose.

c.text: The table combines these properties. **D and n** are both voiced and alveolar, but d is an oral stop and n is a nasal stop.
children: English nasal stops are voiced. Recognizing this organization shows how much structured knowledge is involved in producing ordinary consonants.

c.text: **Artificial intelligence, or AI, models psychological abilities** such as knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. These are abilities found in animals, including humans.
Ideas about human behavior and cognition contribute to AI design. AI therefore has connections to the study of minds and brains, as well as to computing.

c.text: The **cloze procedure** tests completion. Words are removed from a passage, and a reader supplies the missing words.
children: The procedure was developed to measure readability. Completing a passage requires using the words that remain to work out what belongs in the gaps.

c.text: **Closure** is the tendency to perceive a complete familiar pattern even when part of it is missing. The broken circular shapes support the perception of a whole shape that is not fully drawn.
The **cloze procedure** applies completion to language. A reader uses the surrounding words to supply a missing word.
children: Successful completion depends on knowledge of the language. The answer must fit the pattern formed by the available words.

c.text: **Completion** can test knowledge by asking a system to supply a missing part of a sequence. A successful answer shows that the system can use the pattern in the available information.
This approach treats an AI system’s knowledge in terms of its ability to complete sequences. **Prediction** is another way to describe supplying the expected continuation.

c.text: **GPT predicts the next word from the words supplied to it.** Each input word is represented by a **vector**, which is a list of numbers.
children: Different words receive different vectors. The numbers give the computer a representation it can use in calculations.

c.text: The output is a **probability distribution**. It assigns a probability to each possible next word.
children: For “chickens cackle and ducks,” **quack** should receive a high probability. An unrelated continuation such as “cat” should receive a low probability. The output represents several possibilities and how strongly each is predicted.

c.text: **Weights** are numbers that hold the system’s learned knowledge. The input vectors represent the words supplied to the system, and the weights help transform those inputs into predictions.
The calculation uses operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Its output is a **probability distribution** over possible next words.
children: The symbol **x** refers to an input, while **w** refers to a weight. They have different jobs even though both are numbers used in the calculation.

c.text: **Synapses** are connections between neurons in the brain. Knowledge of language involves an enormous network of these connections.
children: Knowing that chickens cackle and ducks quack depends on knowledge held in the brain’s connections. A large number of connections is therefore an important feature of the human system being studied.

c.text: The scale comparison concerns the **large number of connections or weights** in each system. A large number of weights in AI is not, by itself, a reason to dismiss a connection with human knowledge.

c.text: **Prediction** means using available information to anticipate a missing or upcoming part. In a sequence-completion task, predicting the continuation and completing the sequence describe the same task.
Treating knowledge as successful prediction is a proposal about what it means for an AI system to know something. It focuses attention on whether the system can produce an appropriate continuation.

c.text: **Learning from mistakes** means using the difference between a prediction and the appropriate answer to improve the system. Making a prediction provides something that can be checked and corrected.
**Stochastic gradient descent, or SGD**, is a learning algorithm. A simple averaging problem makes its correction process easier to understand without requiring a complicated AI system.

c.text: **Observation-based error learning** starts with an estimate and improves it using individual observations. In the averaging example, the estimate is a guess about the average of a list of numbers.
children: Compare the estimate with one number from the list, then move the estimate partway toward that number. Repeating this with more observations allows the data to shape the estimate.

c.text: The important idea is **improvement through repeated corrections**. The estimate is learned from data instead of being obtained by directly adding the whole list and dividing.

c.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** begins with an estimate, **x**, and compares it with a randomly selected observation, **d**. The difference between them is called the **loss** in this example.
children: Subtracting a small fraction of that difference moves the estimate toward the observation. If the estimate is above the observation, it moves down. If it is below the observation, it moves up.

c.text: The **learning rate** is the fraction used for each correction. A rate of 10% moves the estimate one tenth of the way toward the selected observation.

**Stochastic** refers to the random choice of observations. **Gradient** concerns the direction related to the loss, and **descent** concerns reducing the error. Repeated observations guide the estimate toward the average.

c.text: The **initial condition**, or **IC**, is the starting estimate. The colored curves begin above, near and below the average, so they approach the same region from different directions.
The **learning rate** determines how much each observation changes the estimate.
children: A small rate produces smaller changes. The estimate approaches the average more slowly but fluctuates less.
A larger rate moves the estimate into the right region faster. Each new observation also pulls it farther, producing larger fluctuations around the average.

c.text: The starting estimate and the learning rate affect different aspects of learning. The starting estimate determines where the path begins, while the learning rate changes the size of its corrections.

c.text: The **speed–accuracy tradeoff** concerns how quickly an estimate improves and how precisely it settles near the average.
children: A higher **learning rate**, written **γ**, gives observations more influence. The estimate changes quickly but continues to fluctuate more.
A lower learning rate makes each correction smaller. Learning is slower, but the estimate can remain closer to the average.

c.text: Improving an optimization method means trying to obtain both faster learning and greater accuracy. Changing the learning rate alone creates a tradeoff between those goals in these examples.

c.text: A **dynamical system** can be understood through its **elements**, the **relations** between them and its **goal**. The elements are the parts, and the relations describe how those parts affect one another.
children: The goal identifies what the organized activity accomplishes. Describing the parts alone misses how their interactions produce the behavior of the whole system.

c.text: An octopus keeping its den uses its **eight arms**, the ground and its interactions with a fish as parts of an organized action. Its nervous system is distributed through its head and body.
The **relations** between the arms, ground and fish determine how the movements work together. Their shared **goal** is to keep the den.
children: Understanding the action requires explaining the coordination between parts, rather than treating each arm movement separately.

c.text: **Speech is a dynamical system** because several parts work together over time to convey a thought. Its elements include the tongue, lips, velum, larynx, palate and **pharyngeal wall**, the back wall of the throat.
children: The brain coordinates the relations between these parts. Producing speech depends on how their movements fit together, rather than on one structure acting alone.

c.text: **Dynamical systems** occur throughout the body. Voluntary actions and involuntary activity in the heart, pancreas and neurons all involve parts affecting one another over time.
The elements can be whole organs, parts of organs, cells or chemicals within cells. A system can therefore be studied at different physical scales.
children: Systems with very different elements can share patterns of organization. Recognizing those shared relations helps explain behavior across biology, chemistry and physics.

c.text: A complex octopus action can be analyzed into **motor primitives**, simpler movement components that combine to produce the full action. The slapping action involves coordinated changes in arm movement.

c.text: The important question is how the movement components fit together to achieve the animal’s goal. A description of the separate parts alone does not explain the complete action.

c.text: The **shortest path problem** asks which route has the lowest total cost. A route begins at **A**, passes through states at successive stages and ends at **J**.
children: Each arrow has a cost. A route’s total cost is the sum of the costs of all its arrows.

c.text: The best route depends on the **whole path**. Selecting one inexpensive arrow does not establish that the complete route will have the lowest cost.

c.text: A **greedy algorithm** selects the lowest-cost arrow available at the current state. It repeats that local choice at each stage.
children: A cheap immediate step can lead to an expensive continuation. The algorithm can therefore produce a route whose total cost is higher than another available route.

c.text: The important difference is between the **cost of the next step** and the **total cost of reaching the destination**. Greedy choice based only on the next arrow ignores that distinction.

c.text: An **exhaustive algorithm** checks every possible route and compares their total costs. Checking all possibilities allows it to identify the lowest-cost complete route.
children: The number of routes grows as more stages and states are added. Exhaustive search can therefore take a very long time, even though it finds the correct answer.

c.text: In **dynamic programming**, a state’s **value** is the best total cost of getting from that state to the destination. **V_BJ** means the best cost from B to J, and **V_CJ** means the best cost from C to J.
To find the best cost from A, compare the complete alternatives.
children: For the route through B, add the cost from A to B to the value of B. For the route through C, add the cost from A to C to the value of C.
The smaller total gives the **value of A**. Each comparison includes both the immediate step and the best remaining route.

c.text: The values of B and C are **subproblems** within the problem of finding the value of A. They must be solved before their answers can be used.
children: This is **Bellman’s decomposition**. Break the full problem into smaller problems whose solutions provide the information required by the larger problem.

c.text: The value of B depends on the best costs from **D, E and F** to J. Each possible next step contributes its immediate cost plus the value of the state reached.
At the final stage, **G, H and I** connect directly to J. Their values can be read from those final arrows.
children: Those known values allow the values at the preceding stage to be calculated. Repeating this backward through the network supplies the values required at the start.

c.text: **Calculate the values before choosing the route.** A value includes the best remaining cost, so it contains information missing from the cost of a single arrow.
Starting at A, compare the cost of each possible step **plus the value of the state it reaches**. Choose the alternative with the smallest combined cost.
children: Repeat this at each state until reaching J. The choices are local, but the calculated values make them account for the full remaining route.

c.text: A **state value** summarizes the best total cost from that state to the destination. A costly obstacle near the end of a route therefore affects values calculated at earlier states.
children: This prevents an inexpensive initial arrow from appearing attractive when its continuation is expensive.

c.text: The values are calculated **backward** from the destination. The route is then followed **forward** from the start, using the stored values to select each step.

c.text: **Dynamic programming decomposes a problem into smaller subproblems.** If a subproblem still depends on unknown information, it is broken into smaller problems in turn.
children: The process reaches cases simple enough to solve directly. Their answers are then used to solve the larger problems that depend on them.

c.text: The full solution is built from these smaller solutions. A solved subproblem supplies an answer that can be reused wherever it is needed.

c.text: **Bellman’s rule** calculates a state’s value by comparing its possible continuations. For each next state, add the immediate arrow cost to that next state’s value, then keep the smallest total.
Apply this rule from the last stage toward the first. Each state’s value becomes available when the values it depends on are known.
children: Reusing these values avoids recalculating the same remaining routes for every complete path. This is why **dynamic programming** can be much more efficient than exhaustive search.

c.text: The **lowest total cost** can require choosing a more expensive initial step. That step can lead to a cheaper continuation and avoid a large cost near the end.

The **shortest distance** and **least time** are also different goals. When movement has the same speed everywhere, a straight route is fastest. When running on sand is faster than swimming, spending more of the route on sand can reduce the total time.
children: The best route depends on what is being minimized and on the costs of all its parts.

c.text: **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes between media in which its speed differs. The route taken is a **least-time path**.
children: The fastest complete route can include different distances in the two media. Minimizing travel time is therefore different from requiring the shortest straight-line distance.

c.text: An optimization problem must account for the **total cost across the route**. In the network, a more expensive early arrow can be worthwhile if it avoids a greater cost in the continuation.

c.text: Both graphs show an **approach to equilibrium**, a value toward which the system tends. Estimates that begin above or below the average move toward the same region.
children: For the temperature curves, hot coffee cools and iced coffee warms toward room temperature. The change is larger when the temperature difference is larger and smaller near room temperature.

c.text: The shared pattern is **rapid change far from equilibrium and slower change near it**. The quantities are different, but both graphs describe change toward a stable level.
